The federal minimum wage should be raised significantly to ensure workers can afford basic necessities and participate fully in the economy. At its current level of $7.25 per hour—unchanged since 2009—the minimum wage fails to provide a living wage, trapping millions in poverty despite full-time work. Raising it to at least $15 per hour would align with inflation and productivity growth, reducing income inequality and stimulating consumer spending, which drives economic growth.  

Opponents argue that higher wages could lead to job losses, but evidence from states that have already raised their minimum wages shows minimal employment disruption, offset by increased worker productivity and retention. Businesses benefit from lower turnover and higher morale, while workers gain financial stability, reducing reliance on public assistance.  

My support for this policy stems from a belief in economic justice—no one working full-time should struggle to afford housing, food, or healthcare. A higher minimum wage is a direct step toward correcting decades of wage stagnation and corporate profit growth at the expense of workers. The government has a responsibility to ensure fair compensation, and raising the federal minimum wage is a necessary intervention to create a more equitable economy.
